nameStory: Squashberry gets its name from the rather unfortunate smell and texture of its ripe berries when crushed - they tend to squash easily and release a somewhat unpleasant odor. It's also called mooseberry because moose and other wildlife eagerly munch on both the berries and tender twigs, making it an important food source in northern forests.
description: Squashberry is a medium-sized shrub that grows up to 8 feet tall, forming loose colonies in northern woods. It belongs to the viburnum family, a group of shrubs known for their showy spring flowers and colorful berries. The plant has a somewhat open, irregular growth pattern with smooth branches that spread outward. Like other viburnums, it produces clusters of small white flowers in spring followed by bright red berries that are an important wildlife food.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-lobed leaves that look somewhat like small maple leaves, with coarse teeth along the edges and prominent veins that you can easily feel with your fingertips

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Bright red berries in flat-topped clusters that ripen in late summer, with a tart smell when crushed and a single large flat seed inside

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small creamy-white flowers arranged in flat-topped clusters about 2-4 inches across, with a light sweet fragrance in late spring

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth grayish-brown bark on younger branches that feels almost papery to the touch, becoming slightly rougher with age

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Open, somewhat sprawling shrub that often leans or grows at angles, typically 4-8 feet tall with irregular branching

habitat: Squashberry thrives in cool, moist northern forests, particularly in areas with rich, well-drained soil. In New England, look for it in mixed hardwood-conifer forests, forest edges, and stream valleys, especially at higher elevations in the mountains. It's often found growing alongside other northern species like balsam fir, paper birch, and mountain ash.

seasonality.spring: New leaves unfurl with a fresh green color, and creamy-white flower clusters appear in late May to early June, filling the air with a subtle sweet fragrance.
seasonality.summer: Full foliage provides good identification opportunities with the distinctive three-lobed leaves, while green berries begin forming in flat-topped clusters.
seasonality.fall: Bright red berries ripen and become very noticeable, while leaves may turn yellow or reddish before dropping. This is peak time for wildlife feeding.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the smooth bark and irregular growth pattern, with some dried berry clusters sometimes persisting into early winter.

funFact: Despite being called 'highbush cranberry' or 'lowbush cranberry' in some regions, squashberry isn't related to true cranberries at all - it's actually in the honeysuckle family, and the confusion comes from indigenous peoples using the tart berries similarly to cranberries for food and medicine.
confusionNotes: Squashberry is most easily confused with guelder-rose (Viburnum opulus), another viburnum with similar three-lobed leaves and red berries. The key difference is that guelder-rose has much more deeply cut leaf lobes and the berries have a distinctly bitter, almost medicinal smell when crushed, while squashberry berries smell more generically tart.
contextualKnowledge: The alternate names 'moosewood viburnum' and 'pembina' reflect its importance to both wildlife and indigenous cultures - 'pembina' comes from the Ojibwe word for the berries, and many northern communities have traditionally used the fruit for jams and sauces despite the need to remove the large, bitter seeds first.
compareHints: Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns. Hobblebush has much larger, heart-shaped leaves, while the arrowwoods have simple toothed leaves without lobes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
